Honors Algebra 2 · Topic 2 · Lessons 2.3 – 2.6

Solving Quadratics, One Step at a Time

Completing the square, vertex form, writing quadratics from their zeros, the Quadratic Formula, and the discriminant. Each step builds on the one before it, so go in order.

0
Step 0

Warm-up toolkit

Four small skills that show up in every problem in this guide. Get these solid first.

The four tools

1. Square roots come in pairs. If x2=49, then x=±7, because 72 and (−7)2 both equal 49. Forget the ± and you lose half the answer.

2. Simplify radicals by pulling out the biggest perfect square: 48​=16⋅3​=43​.

3. Square root of a negative uses i=−1​: −25​=5i and −18​=9​⋅2​⋅i=3i2​.

4. Perfect square trinomials factor into a binomial squared: x2+14x+49=(x+7)2. The pattern is x2+2px+p2=(x+p)2.

Solve: x2=81
Check answer

x=±9 (so x=9 or x=−9)

Hint

1
Step 1

Solve with square roots

If one side of the equation is already a perfect square, you can skip factoring and just take the square root of both sides.

Key idea

Get the equation into the form (x+p)2=q. Then take ± ​ of both sides and solve for x.

(x+p)2=q⟹x+p=±q​⟹x=−p±q​

Watch me

Solve 25=x2+14x+49.

25=x2+14x+49
Spot it: x2+14x+49 is a perfect square trinomial (half of 14 is 7, and 72=49).
25=(x+7)2
Rewrite the right side as a binomial squared.
±5=x+7
Square root of both sides. Don't forget the ±!
x+7=5orx+7=−5
Split into two equations.
x=−2orx=−12
Subtract 7 from each.
Solutions: x=−2 and x=−12

2
Step 2

Build a perfect square

Most quadratics aren't perfect squares. Completing the square means adding the one number that turns them into one.

See it as a picture

Think of x2+bx as area. Cut the bx rectangle in half and put one half on each side of the x2 square.

Now there's a missing corner. It measures 2b​ by 2b​, so its area is (2b​)2.

Add that corner and you get a full square with side x+2b​.

The magic number

x2+bx+(2b​)2=(x+2b​)2

In words: take the middle coefficient, cut it in half, square it. Add that.

Bonus: the number inside the parentheses is just half of b, the step before you squared it. Write it down, because you'll need it.

Keep it balanced

In an equation, whatever you add to one side, you add to the other. Completing the square is legal only because you add the same amount to both sides.

Watch me

Write x2+8x+5=0 in the form (x+p)2=q.

x2+8x=−5
Move the constant to the other side. Make room for the magic number.
28​=4,42=16
Half of b, then square it.
x2+8x+16=−5+16
Add 16 to both sides.
(x+4)2=11
Left side factors using half of b (that's 4). Right side: −5+16=11.

3
Step 3

Complete the square to solve

Now put Steps 1 and 2 together. Build the perfect square, then solve it with square roots.

The 5-step recipe (when a=1)

  1. Move the constant to the right side: x2+bx=number
  2. Find the magic number: (2b​)2
  3. Add it to both sides
  4. Factor the left side as (x+2b​)2 and simplify the right
  5. Square root both sides (±!) and solve for x
Watch me

Solve 0=x2−2x+3 by completing the square.

−3=x2−2x
Move: subtract 3 from both sides.
(2−2​)2=(−1)2=1
Find the magic number.
−3+1=x2−2x+1
Add 1 to both sides.
−2=(x−1)2
Factor. Half of b was −1, so it's (x−1)2.
±−2​=x−1
Square root. Negative inside? That means i.
±i2​=x−1
−2​=i2​
x=1±i2​
Add 1 to both sides.
x=1+i2​ and x=1−i2​

Square root: ±00​=x+2→x=00000​

Check answer

−8=x2+4x→4→−4=(x+2)2→±2i=x+2→x=−2±2i

4
Step 4

When a=1

The magic-number trick only works when the x2 term has a coefficient of 1. So make it 1 first.

One extra step at the start

Step 0: Divide every term by a. Then run the same 5-step recipe from Step 3.

Yes, this usually creates fractions. That's normal. Keep them as fractions (not decimals) and you'll be fine.

Watch me

Solve 2x2=6x−20.

x2=3x−10
Divide every term by 2.
x2−3x=−10
Move so the x terms are together on the left and the constant is on the right.
(2−3​)2=49​
Find the magic number.
x2−3x+49​=−440​+49​
Add to both sides. Rewrite −10 as −440​ so you can add fractions.
(x−23​)2=−431​
Factor.
x−23​=±2i31​​
Square root. 4​=2 in the bottom, and the negative gives i.
x=23​±2i31​​
Add 23​.

5
Step 5

Vertex form & max/min

Completing the square on a function turns standard form into vertex form, which tells you the vertex (the max or min) right away.

From standard form to vertex form

y=ax2+bx+c⟶y=a(x−h)2+k

The vertex is (h,k). If a>0 the parabola opens up and k is a minimum. If a<0 it opens down and k is a maximum.

The big difference from solving: you factor out a instead of dividing by it, because there's no "other side" to divide.

Watch me

Write y=−2x2+10x+1 in vertex form. Find the max or min.

y−1=−2x2+10x
Move the constant to the y side.
y−1=−2(x2−5x)
Factor out a=−2. Now the inside has a=1.
(2−5​)2=6.25
Magic number for the inside.
y−1+(−2)(6.25)=−2(x2−5x+6.25)
Adding 6.25 inside really adds −2×6.25=−12.5. So add −12.5 to the left.
y−13.5=−2(x−2.5)2
Simplify and factor.
y=−2(x−2.5)2+13.5
Add 13.5 to both sides.

a=−2<0, so it opens down.
Maximum of 13.5 at x=2.5

Common error

Adding 6.25 to the left side. The 6.25 went inside parentheses that are being multiplied by −2, so the amount you actually added was −2(6.25)=−12.5. Always multiply the magic number by the a you factored out.

a>0, so it has a max / min​ of 00​ at x=00​

6
Step 6

Word problems

Real problems come as stories. Your job: turn the story into a quadratic equation, then use the tools you already have.

Story → equation checklist

  1. Name your variables (what is x, t, w?)
  2. Write an equation for each fact in the story
  3. Substitute to get one equation with one variable
  4. Solve (complete the square, or any method)
  5. Answer the question in a sentence with units. Throw out answers that make no sense (negative time, negative length).
Watch me

A rancher has 340 m of fencing for a rectangular pasture and wants an area of 6,000 m². What dimensions should she use?

2ℓ+2w=340
Perimeter fact. Let ℓ = length, w = width.
ℓ=170−w
Divide by 2 and solve for ℓ.
ℓw=6000
Area fact.
(170−w)w=6000
Substitute for ℓ.
w2−170w=−6000
Distribute, then multiply everything by −1 so a=1.
w2−170w+7225=1225
Magic number: (−85)2=7225. Add to both sides.
(w−85)2=1225
Factor.
w−85=±35
1225​=35
w=120 or w=50
If w=50, then ℓ=120 (and the other way around).
The pasture should be 120 m by 50 m.

6.1
A ball's height is h=32t−16t2+4 (feet, after t seconds). When does it reach 20 ft?

Set h=20: 20=32t−16t2+4

Get everything on one side: 16t2−32t+00​=0

Divide by 16: t2−2t+0​=0

That's already a perfect square: (t−0​)2=0

So t=0​ second

Check answer

16t2−32t+16=0→t2−2t+1=0→(t−1)2=0→t=1 second.

Only one answer means 20 ft is the very top of the throw: the ball touches 20 ft once, then comes down.

7
Step 7

Write a quadratic from its zeros

This is solving in reverse. You're given the answers and asked to build the equation.

Key idea

If the zeros are r1​ and r2​, then y=(x−r1​)(x−r2​). Multiply it out to get standard form.

Watch the signs: a zero of 3 gives the factor (x−3). A zero of −5 gives (x−(−5))=(x+5).

Conjugate pairs travel together

If a quadratic with integer coefficients has a zero like 3−i or 1+5​, its conjugate (3+i or 1−5​) is also a zero. Shortcut for multiplying conjugate pairs: (x−r1​)(x−r2​)=x2−(sum)x+(product).

Watch me

Write a quadratic in standard form with zeros x=3 and x=−5.

y=(x−3)(x+5)
Turn each zero into a factor. Signs flip!
y=x2+5x−3x−15
FOIL (multiply every term by every term).
y=x2+2x−15
Combine like terms.

8
Step 8

The Quadratic Formula

If you complete the square on ax2+bx+c=0 using letters instead of numbers, you get a formula that solves every quadratic.

Memorize this

x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

Works for any ax2+bx+c=0 with a=0. The equation must equal 0 first.

Where it comes from (it's just Step 4 with letters)

ax2+bx+c=0
Start.
x2+ab​x=−ac​
Divide by a, move the constant.
x2+ab​x+(2ab​)2=−ac​+4a2b2​
Add the magic number: half of ab​, squared.
(x+2ab​)2=4a2b2−4ac​
Factor; combine fractions on the right.
x+2ab​=±2ab2−4ac​​
Square root both sides.
x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​
Subtract 2ab​. Done!
Watch me

Solve 3x2−4x−9=0.

a=3,b=−4,c=−9
Label a, b, c. Keep the signs!
x=2(3)−(−4)±(−4)2−4(3)(−9)​​
Plug in with parentheses around every value.
x=64±16+108​​=64±124​​
Simplify. Notice −4(3)(−9)=+108.
x=64±231​​
124​=4⋅31​=231​
x=32±31​​
Every term divides by 2. Reduce.

Common errors

• (−4)2=16, but −42 on a calculator is −16. Use parentheses.

• The fraction bar goes under the whole top, −b included, not just the square root.

• To reduce, every term on top must divide by the same number as the bottom.

9
Step 9

The discriminant

The part under the square root, b2−4ac, tells you what kind of answers you'll get before you do any solving.

Discriminant =b2−4ac

It's called the discriminant because it discriminates, or sorts, quadratics into three kinds.

b2−4ac>0
2 real solutions
crosses the x-axis twice
e.g. x2+x−2=0
b2−4ac=0
1 real solution
touches the x-axis once
e.g. x2−4x+4=0
b2−4ac<0
2 non-real solutions
never touches the x-axis
e.g. x2−3x+3=0
Watch me

A tennis ball's height is h(t)=−5t2+5t+2 (meters). Will it reach 4 m?

−5t2+5t+2=4
Set the height equal to 4.
−5t2+5t−2=0
Make it =0. Now a=−5,b=5,c=−2.
(5)2−4(−5)(−2)=25−40=−15
Find the discriminant.
−15<0
Negative means no real solution, so there's no real time when h=4.
No, the ball never reaches 4 m.

Volleyball check

A jump serve leaves the hand on a path modeled by h=−4.9t2+8t+2 (meters). Without solving, can the ball reach 6 m? What about 5 m?

Check answer

6 m: −4.9t2+8t−4=0. Discriminant =64−78.4=−14.4<0. No.

10
Step 10

Mixed review: pick a method

On a test, nobody tells you which method to use. Every method gives the same answer, but some are much faster.

If the equation looks like…Try…Why
(x+p)2=q or x2=qSquare rootsAlready done for you. Take ± ​.
Easy-to-factor numbersFactoringFastest when it works.
a=1 and b is evenCompleting the squareNo fractions. Clean.
You need the vertex / max / minCompleting the squareGives vertex form directly.
Messy numbers, or nothing else worksQuadratic FormulaAlways works, every time.
"How many / what kind of solutions?"DiscriminantNo need to fully solve.
On your own

Describe the number and type of solutions of 2x2+7x+11=0.
Check answer

49−88=−39<0, so two non-real solutions.

On your own
10.2
Solve x2−8x+16=0. Is the Quadratic Formula the only way? Explain.
Check answer

x=4 (one real solution). Not the only way: it's a perfect square, (x−4)2=0, so factoring or square roots is faster.

10.3
Rick says x2+5x+9=0 has no solution. Jenny says it has two. How could both be right?
Check answer

Discriminant =25−36=−11<0. Rick is right that there are no real solutions (the graph never crosses the x-axis). Jenny is right that there are two complex (non-real) solutions.

Check answer

(x+5)2=3→x=−5±3​. Square roots is fastest here since the left side is already a perfect square.

One-glance summary

Magic number: (2b​)2. Only use it when a=1. Add it to both sides.

a=1: divide by a when solving. Factor out a for vertex form (and multiply the magic number by a on the other side).

Vertex form: y=a(x−h)2+k, vertex (h,k). a>0: min. a<0: max.

From zeros: y=(x−r1​)(x−r2​). Irrational and complex zeros come in conjugate pairs.

Quadratic Formula: x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​. Set the equation equal to 0 first.

Discriminant b2−4ac: positive gives 2 real, zero gives 1 real, negative gives 2 non-real.
